lessons.situation: A repair visit has been confirmed with both the tenant and the contractor, the appointment time has passed, and no completion report or work results have come back.
lessons.action: Do not close the job or assume the works were done. Place the job on hold as 'waiting on response' and chase the contractor for an outcome of the visit (attended or not, work done, follow-up needed). Check with the tenant if the contractor stays silent, and review the job again once a reply arrives.
lessons.rationale: Without a completion report from the contractor, the real status of the visit is unknown, so the job must stay open and be actively followed up rather than progressed or closed.

lessons.situation: After a plumbing visit was booked and confirmed with the tenant and contractor, the contractor's email reply could not be parsed by the system and was flagged for manual review, with no usable content available.
lessons.action: When a provider's email cannot be extracted, manually review the original message or check with the contractor directly to establish what it said. If it indicates the job is complete, move the task to the results/closeout stage. Put the job on hold with the reason 'Waiting for Provider' and note that the contractor reports completion and the invoice is awaited. Do not treat the unreadable email as a no-op or re-send appointment messages.
lessons.rationale: An unparseable contractor email may contain a completion notice or other status change, so a human check keeps the task in the right stage and ensures the invoice is chased rather than lost.

lessons.situation: A provider has been assigned after landlord approval and has made contact attempts with the tenant (a callback request and a failed call connection), but no booking has been confirmed and nothing in the contact requires an agency reply.
lessons.action: Review the provider's contact attempts to see whether they ask the agency for anything. If they only concern arranging access with the tenant and need no agency response, do not intervene or send new messages. Put the job on hold with the reason 'waiting for provider' and a note that the appointment is still to be booked, then let the provider and tenant sort out the visit and revisit if no booking is confirmed.
lessons.rationale: Provider-tenant call attempts are a normal part of scheduling and need no agency action, so holding with a clear note avoids duplicate chasing while keeping the job visible until the appointment is booked.

lessons.situation: A contractor has been assigned to a repair and left a voicemail for the tenant to arrange access, then the system prompts the operator to decide whether a response to the provider is needed or to return the job to auto mode.
lessons.action: Don't return the job to auto mode yet. Text the tenant (twice if needed) to say the contractor has tried to reach them and give the contractor's direct number so they can call back. Put the job on hold and ask the contractor by email, with a matching SMS nudge, whether the tenant has got back to them.
lessons.rationale: A voicemail alone doesn't confirm that a booking has been made, so nudging the tenant and checking in with the contractor keeps scheduling moving and stops the job stalling unnoticed in auto mode.

lessons.situation: A confirmed repair visit has passed (a second attempt after an earlier failed fix) and the system has flagged that no work results or completion update have been received from the contractor.
lessons.action: Review the case thread to see whether the contractor has sent any message that still needs a reply from the agency. If nothing is outstanding, return the request to auto mode so the standard chasers for completion or results continue, and do not escalate or re-book manually.
lessons.rationale: A missing work result often just means the contractor's update has not arrived yet, so the first step is to confirm whether the ball is in the agency's court before intervening, and otherwise let automation resume the follow-up.
